svg.title: When to move from one authorization model to the next
svg.desc: Four steps, each taken only when a need appears. Roles, the default of init, while rights follow job functions. Roles and instance policies when a few rules need the loaded element. Relationships with tuples in your own database, written in the transaction, when rights are shared per element. A dedicated engine such as OpenFGA when a measured need appears: an actor reaching too many tuples, a second service asking the same questions, a consistency requirement. Apart from the steps, rules owned and reviewed outside the code point to Cedar or Open Policy Agent behind the same port.
svg.text: When to move from one model to the next: only when a need appears
1. Roles
RoleBasedAuthorizer, the default of init
rights follow job functions:
patient, practitioner, administrator
when a few rules need the loaded element
2. Roles and instance policies
the access facade asks the policies, then the roles
only the patient who booked, or the practitioner,
may cancel: still no tuple store
when rights are shared per element
3. Relationships in your database
RelationBasedAuthorizer, tuples in the transaction
delegated assistants, practices owning calendars:
what the example application does
when a measure says so: an actor reaches too many tuples,
a second service asks, a consistency requirement
4. A dedicated engine
@ddd-ts-kit/openfga, or SpiceDB by hand
a stateful service on the path of every request,
tuples written after the commit
Another axis: who writes the rules
rules owned and reviewed outside the code, by a security team:
Cedar or Open Policy Agent behind the same port, with attributes supplied by a projection
